vignette:
He is 62, a professional dancer who has spent most of his life trusting his body before he trusts words. He and his wife have built their days around rehearsals, performances, teaching, and the quiet rituals that keep him limber enough to keep moving in a career that asks a lot from an aging body. Before the accident, he describes himself as someone who noticed rhythm everywhere-the hiss of a bus door, the tapping of rain on a window, the syncopated sounds of traffic in the city. He moved through the world with confidence, alert but not afraid.

The collision happens late one evening as he is driving home after teaching. He is tired in the ordinary way, his dance bag in the passenger seat, his mind drifting between corrections he gave a student and what his wife might have made for dinner. At an intersection, another car comes fast through a light. He remembers the impossible brightness of headlights, then the violent crush of metal folding inward. He says time does something strange in those seconds. He hears glass explode, feels the seat belt wrench across his chest, smells gasoline and hot plastic, and is certain, with a clarity that still unsettles him, that he is about to die.

For a few moments after the impact, he cannot understand whether he is conscious. He tries to move his legs first. As a dancer, that is his first thought-not abstract survival, but whether his legs are still there, whether his spine is intact, whether the body that has carried him through decades has just been taken from him. He hears someone shouting outside. His hands are shaking so badly he cannot undo his seat belt. Later he learns he survives with injuries that heal, but what stays with him is the terror of being trapped in the car, waiting for help, listening to the engine tick and fearing it will ignite.

In the first weeks afterward, everyone around him focuses on how fortunate he is. He nods and says the same thing. He tells friends he is lucky to be alive. He goes to medical appointments, follows instructions, tries to return to the studio carefully. On the surface, he looks disciplined, determined, even grateful. But his wife notices he startles violently at sudden sounds. If a tray drops in the kitchen, he jerks and grabs the counter. At night he sleeps in fragments. He wakes with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, sometimes already halfway out of bed, as if he needs to escape something before he is fully awake. In his dreams, there is always the light coming toward him.

As his body recovers, his world grows smaller. He avoids driving through intersections, then avoids driving at all. At first he asks his wife to take the wheel "just for now," but soon he invents reasons not to go out unless absolutely necessary. Riding as a passenger is not much easier. He scans every car coming from the side, presses his foot into the floorboard as if he can brake, and grips the door handle hard enough to leave his hand aching. He knows his reactions seem excessive. That awareness does not stop them.

The studio, once his safest place, becomes unpredictable. Mirrors catch sudden flashes of motion that mimic the oncoming headlights. Music with heavy percussion can make his chest tighten. During rehearsal, if another dancer moves too quickly into his peripheral vision, his body flinches before his mind can correct it. He is embarrassed by this. Dance has always been where he feels precise and composed; now he loses counts, forgets combinations he has taught for years, and sometimes goes blank in the middle of demonstrating a phrase. He covers with humor, but inside he feels betrayed by his own mind.

He also finds himself altered at home in ways that are harder to explain. He is more irritable, quicker to snap, then ashamed a moment later. His wife asks simple questions and he hears them as demands. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks routes in advance, looking for roads with fewer intersections. He used to love evening drives with music playing and the windows down; now even seeing skid marks on pavement is enough to turn his stomach. There are days he tells himself he should be over it by now, that at his age he should know how to be strong. Instead, he feels weak and on guard at the same time.

What troubles him most is that the accident does not stay in the past. It returns uninvited-in the glare of sunlight on a windshield, in the smell of overheated brakes, in the split second when a car rolls too quickly toward a cross street. In those moments he is no longer a man on his way to rehearsal or sitting beside his wife. He is back in the driver's seat, trapped in twisted metal, waiting to find out if he lives. Even now, months later, he speaks about the collision with a dancer's awareness of the body: how fear lives in his chest, how tension gathers in his shoulders, how his breath shortens without permission. He says he survived the crash, but part of him still moves through the world as if impact is always one second away.
